title-group.article-title: Sintilimab (PD-1 inhibitor) plus lenvatinib as conversion therapy followed by sequential surgery (SILENSES) for advanced unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a phase II, expansion trial

abstract.p: Our previous findings demonstrated the promising antitumor activity and manageable safety of sintilimab-lenvatinib conversion therapy. The current study aimed to evaluate long-term survival outcomes in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) who underwent sequential surgical resection after successful conversion therapy. In this prospective, single-arm, expansion, phase II trial, patients with unresectable HCC received lenvatinib plus sintilimab conversion therapy. Hepatectomy was performed in consenting patients after successful conversion therapy. The primary endpoint was the conversion rate; secondary endpoints included median overall survival (OS), 5-year survival rates, and recurrence-free survival (RFS). Successful conversion was achieved in 67 of 120 patients (56%, 67/120). Independent imaging review per mRECIST and RECIST v1.1 criteria demonstrated objective response rates of 58.3% (70/120) and 45.8% (55/120), respectively. With a median follow-up of 41.0 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 39.5–42.5) for the entire cohort, the median OS was 36.0 months (95% CI, 25.0 to not estimable [NE]), with a 5-year OS rate of 42.6% (95% CI, 34.0–53.0). Following multidisciplinary team evaluation and consideration of patient preferences, 60 patients underwent surgical resection, achieving a median RFS of 40.0 months (95% CI, 24.0 to NE) and a 5-year survival rate of 73.9% (95% CI, 62.7–87.1). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 37 patients (31%). Approximately half of the patients with unresectable HCC achieved successful conversion after sintilimab plus lenvatinib therapy. Among those who achieved successful conversion, subsequent curative surgery demonstrated not only a favorable safety profile but also significant survival benefits. Trial registration number: ChiCTR1900023914.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) constitutes a leading global cause of cancer-related mortality, with a particularly high prevalence in East Asia.1 Surgical resection with curative intent remains the optimal strategy for achieving long-term survival, with 5-year survival rates of 50–70% reported in patients with early-stage disease.2 However, owing to the insidious onset of symptoms, over 50% of HCC cases are diagnosed at advanced stages, rendering systemic therapies the primary treatment modality for this patient population.3

The combination of atezolizumab and bevacizumab constitutes a landmark advancement in HCC therapeutics. In the pivotal IMbrave150 trial, this regimen demonstrated a 29.8% objective response rate (ORR) and a 5.8-month improvement in median overall survival (OS) compared with sorafenib in patients with unresectable HCC.4,5 Strikingly, nearly half of the ongoing clinical trials evaluating combination therapies for HCC involve immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) paired with multikinase inhibitors—with lenvatinib being the most extensively investigated agent in this category—highlighting the substantial therapeutic potential of this strategy.3 Given that the ORR associated with such combination regimens can reach 30–50%, it offers the opportunity for subsequent surgical intervention in patients with initially unresectable HCC.6–8

Conversion therapy has emerged as a paradigm-shifting strategy for patients with initially unresectable HCC, enabling surgical candidacy through multimodal therapeutic approaches that convert unresectable tumors to resectable status. This therapeutic paradigm has catalyzed a rapid expansion of clinical investigations.9–11 However, current evidence on conversion therapy for HCC primarily derives from retrospective studies with inherent limitations, including restricted sample sizes, heterogeneous treatment protocols, and insufficient follow-up durations. These methodological constraints have engendered ongoing controversies regarding optimal therapeutic strategies and clinical end points in this evolving field.

In our previous study investigating conversion therapy for unresectable HCC, the lenvatinib plus anti-PD-1 antibody regimen manifested promising efficacy and acceptable safety profiles.12 Among 56 enrolled patients, the ORR reached 53.6% by mRECIST criteria and 44.6% per RECIST 1.1.12 Successful conversion was achieved in 31 patients, of whom 21 underwent subsequent resection with an R0 resection rate of 85.7% and pathologic complete response (pCR) rate of 38.1%.12 The current study extends this investigation through three key methodological enhancements: expanded cohort enrollment, adoption of a fixed-combination regimen (sintilimab plus lenvatinib), and extended follow-up duration. These refinements aim to rigorously evaluate the long-term survival benefits and therapeutic durability of this conversion strategy.

sec.title: Characteristics of the patients
sec.p:
From July 2019 to May 2023, this prospective cohort study consecutively screened 286 patients with HCC. After excluding 168 individuals based on predefined enrollment criteria, 120 treatment-naïve patients with radiologically confirmed unresectable HCC received conversion therapy comprising sintilimab (200 mg IV Q3W) and lenvatinib (body weight–based oral dosing) (Fig. 1). In this cohort, the majority of patients presented with advanced-stage HCC features (Table 1): over 80% exhibited macrovascular invasion at initial diagnosis, and over 90% were classified as BCLC stage C. Approximately half demonstrated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels exceeding 400 ng/mL, while 33% had extrahepatic metastases. Additionally, more than 80% of the cohort were male with concurrent hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, more than 70% had concomitant liver cirrhosis, and over 90% exhibited Child‒Pugh class A liver function.Fig. 1

sec.title: The conversion rate of systemic therapy
sec.p:
Radiologic assessment per mRECIST and RECIST v1.1 criteria demonstrated target lesion size reduction in 93% (101/109) and 90% (100/111) of evaluable patients, respectively (Fig. 2a, b). The ORR by independent imaging review (IIR) was 58% (70/120) and 46% (55/120) for each criterion. Sixty-seven (56%, 67/120) achieved successful conversion. After MDT evaluation integrated with patient-centered decision-making, 60 (90%, 60/67) of these conversion responders underwent curative-intent hepatectomy. Notably, 85% (51/60) of the surgical group achieved curative resection criteria within 2–5 months (median 3.2 months) of protocol-directed conversion therapy. Among patients with successful conversion therapy, the median number of systemic treatment cycles administered was 5 (range 3–10), with a median treatment duration of 3.5 months (range 2–9) (Supplementary Fig. 1). Furthermore, five protocol-compliant responders experienced nonmedical treatment delays—despite meeting conversion-success standards within 48 weeks, their therapeutic trajectories extended to 14–30 months (median 19 months).Fig. 2
Radiographic tumor response. a Percentage change from baseline in the sum of target lesion diameters according to modified RECIST (mRECIST) criteria among 109 evaluable patients; b Percentage change from baseline in the sum of target lesion diameters per RECIST version 1.1 criteria among 111 evaluable patients. Fisher’s exact test between conversion success and radiographic response assessment, stratified by c mRECIST criteria and d RECIST version 1.1 criteria

Per the mRECIST criteria, three patients with complete radiologic regression of target lesions (100% reduction) were deemed conversion failures. This determination stemmed from protocol deviations: two underwent nonprotocol-specified local therapies during systemic treatment, while one developed new extrahepatic lesions.

Among 21 of 53 patients failing conversion therapy, salvage locoregional interventions, including transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC), radiofrequency ablation (RFA), or radiotherapy, were administered following MDT review of tumor profiles and topographic feasibility. Achievement of successful conversion in initially unresectable HCC patients showed a statistically significant correlation with imaging-assessed treatment response under both mRECIST and RECIST v1.1 criteria (Fisher’s exact test, P < 0.001) (Fig. 2c, d).

Pathologic response stratification revealed 21 (35%, 21/60) patients with pathologic complete response (pCR, 0% residual viable tumor), 25 (42%, 25/60) with pathologic partial response (pPR, ≤50% residual viable tumor), and 14 (23%, 14/60) with pathologic nonresponse (pNR, >50% residual viable tumor) (Table 2).

sec.title: Survival
sec.p:
With a median follow-up of 41 months (95% CI, 39.5–42.5) for the entire cohort, 64 deaths (53%, 64/120) were recorded. Kaplan‒Meier estimates confirmed 12-, 36-, and 60-month survival rates of 70.8% (95% CI, 63.2–79.5), 49.1% (95% CI, 40.6 to 59.3), and 42.6% (95% CI, 34.0–53.4), respectively. The median OS was 36 months (95% CI, 25 to not estimable [NE]) (Fig. 3a).Fig. 3
Survival in the cohort population. a Overall survival in the entire cohort population; b Comparison of overall survival between the surgical and nonsurgical groups. NE not estimable, OS overall survival

Subgroup survival analysis revealed significantly prolonged OS in the surgical group, with estimated 12-, 36-, and 60-month survival rates of 93.3% (95% CI, 87.2–99.9), 79.2% (95% CI, 69.3–90.5), and 73.9% (95% CI, 62.7–87.1), respectively. In contrast, the nonsurgical group exhibited corresponding survival rates of 48.3% (95% CI, 37.2–62.8), 20.0% (95% CI, 11.8–33.9), and NE, with a median OS of only 12 months (95% CI, 10–25) (Fig. 3b). A total of 14 patients (23%) in the surgical group and 50 (83%) in the nonsurgical group died (stratified hazard ratio for death, 0.15; 95% CI, 0.08–0.28; P < 0.001) (Fig. 3b). Of note, baseline clinical characteristics were comparable between the surgical and nonsurgical groups (Table 1).

To avoid immortal time bias, landmark analysis demonstrated that patients who underwent sequential surgical treatment after successful conversion had significantly longer OS than those in the nonsurgical group (stratified hazard ratio for death, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.13–0.43; P < 0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 2).

Furthermore, patients in the successful conversion group also had longer OS than those in the unsuccessful conversion group (stratified hazard ratio for death, 0.15; 95% CI, 0.09–0.26; P < 0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 3a). The baseline characteristics of both groups are detailed in Supplementary Table 1. Exploratory analysis identified that nonsurgical patients achieving successful conversion (n = 7) exhibited inferior survival compared with the surgical group (adjusted P = 0.081) but superior outcomes relative to conversion failure patients (adjusted P = 0.056) (Supplementary Fig. 3b).

Univariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis identified AFP decline during conversion therapy (HR 0.529, 95% CI, 0.406–0.688, P < 0.001), maximal tumor shrinkage ratio (RECIST v1.1: HR 0.068, 95% CI, 0.024–0.194, P < 0.001; mRECIST: HR 0.096, 95% CI, 0.04–0.231, P < 0.001), and surgical intervention (HR 0.152, 95% CI, 0.083–0.277, P < 0.001) as protective factors for OS. Conversely, baseline maximum tumor diameter (HR 1.055, 95% CI, 1.005–1.107, P = 0.031), PVTT grading (HR 1.242, 95% CI, 1.032–1.494, P = 0.022), and radiologic response categories (RECIST v1.1: HR 2.891, 95% CI, 1.93–4.332, P < 0.001; mRECIST: HR 2.622, 95% CI, 1.886 to 3.644, P < 0.001) emerged as significant risk factors for mortality (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis identified decreased AFP during conversion therapy (HR 0.58, 95% CI, 0.414–0.812, P < 0.01) and surgical intervention after successful conversion (HR 0.23, 95% CI, 0.11–0.483, P < 0.001) as independent protective factors for OS in patients with HCC (Supplementary Fig. 4b).

Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) analysis, used to balance patient characteristics between the surgical and nonsurgical groups, demonstrated a more significant survival benefit in the surgical group than in the nonsurgical group (Supplementary Fig. 5a-b). This finding aligns with the generally well-balanced baseline characteristics observed between the two groups.

Two patients underwent R1 resection due to incomplete tumor resection, and the median postoperative follow-up duration for the remaining 58 patients was 38 months (95% CI, 35.7–40.3). Recurrence events occurred in 26 patients (45%, 26/58), with Kaplan‒Meier estimated RFS rates of 72.0% (95% CI, 61.2–84.6), 53.0% (95% CI, 40.8–68.9), and 45.4% (95% CI, 30.5–67.8) at 12, 36, and 48 months post-operatively, respectively. The median RFS was 40 months (95% CI, 24 to not NE) (Supplementary Fig. 6). Univariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis identified depth of pathologic response as the sole risk factor for both OS (HR 4.584, 95% CI, 1.923–10.93, P < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 7a) and RFS (HR 2.526, 95% CI, 1.457–4.381, P < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 7b) in the surgical group.

Survival analysis indicated statistically significant differences in OS across all pairwise comparisons of the pCR, pPR, and pNR subgroups (adjusted P < 0.05 for each) (Supplementary Fig. 8a). In contrast, RFS exhibited significant disparities only between pCR vs. pNR (adjusted P < 0.01) and pPR vs. pNR (adjusted P = 0.013) (Supplementary Fig. 8b). According to the established major pathological response (MPR) criterion (defined as at least 70% nonviable tumor cells)13, we compared outcomes among the MPR subgroup and patients with pCR, pPR, or pNR as defined in our study. The MPR subgroup demonstrated significantly superior OS and RFS compared to the pNR subgroup (adjusted P < 0.01) but showed no significant difference in outcomes compared to the pCR and pPR subgroups (Supplementary Fig. 9a-b).

Intriguingly, according to the mRECIST criteria, pCR was observed in 63% (12/19) of tumors achieving radiological CR, while only 25% (8/32) of PR-associated tumors and 12% (1/8) of SD-associated tumors attained pCR (Supplementary Table 2). By RECIST v1.1 criteria, pCR rates were 41% (16/39) in PR-associated tumors compared with 25% (5/20) in SD-associated tumors (Supplementary Table 3).

sec.title: Adverse events and surgical complications
sec.p: Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 110 patients (92%, 110/120) during conversion therapy, with 37 patients (31%, 37/120) experiencing grade 3–5 TRAEs. The most common all-grade TRAEs included hypertension (40%, 48/120), rash (30%, 36/120), hand-foot syndrome (28%, 34/120), pyrexia (13%, 16/120), and nausea (10%, 12/120). Four patients (3%, 4/120) developed grade 4 immune-related myocarditis: two isolated cases, one concurrent with hypophysitis, and one accompanied by upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Four fatal (3%, 4/120) (grade 5) events occurred: two immune-related myocarditis cases, one gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and one complex case involving immune-related hepatitis, massive ascites, and indeterminate-cause mortality (postmortem evaluation precluded by COVID-19 quarantine restrictions).

Among surgical patients, four patients (7%, 4/60) experienced Clavien‒Dindo grade III postoperative complications, and 10 (17%, 10/60) developed grade IV complications. No mortality was attributed to surgical complications.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Recent systemic therapeutic advances in HCC have driven a proliferation of conversion therapy research targeting advanced-stage and initially unresectable HCC.10,11,14 However, no prior investigation has reported 5-year survival outcomes following conversion therapy combined with curative-intent surgical resection—a critical gap addressed by our expansion analysis. The primary objectives of our trial were to investigate the success rate of conversion therapy using combined immune checkpoint inhibition and targeted therapy in patients with initially unresectable HCC and to assess long-term survival outcomes among conversion responders undergoing resection.

Although no clinical trials investigating sintilimab combined with lenvatinib have been conducted to date in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC, multiple studies have demonstrated promising efficacy of sintilimab and lenvatinib in combination with other therapeutic agents.15–19 In our previous study, sintilimab-lenvatinib combination therapy revealed favorable feasibility and conversion efficacy.12 Through extended follow-up and expanded cohort size, we provide preliminary evidence that sintilimab-lenvatinib combination therapy achieves a 56% (67/120) conversion success rate in patients with unresectable HCC. The cohort achieved a median overall survival of 36 months (95% CI: 25 to not reached) with a 5-year overall survival rate of 42.6% (95% CI: 34.0–53.4).

The LEAP-002 trial reported that the lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab group demonstrated an ORR of 27.8% (95% CI: 23.5–32.6) by investigator review per RECIST v1.1 and 40.8% (95% CI: 35.9–45.8) by blinded independent central review per mRECIST.20 In a phase II clinical trial for advanced HCC, the combination of lenvatinib, sintilimab, and TACE achieved an ORR of 60% per mRECIST and 30% per RECIST v1.1.19 In our cohort, the ORR by IIR was 58% per mRECIST and 46% per RECIST v1.1, which is modestly higher than previously reported studies. Existing research has shown that the high prevalence of HBV infection in Chinese HCC patients is associated with improved response and tolerance to lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab therapy compared to global populations.20 The hepatitis B infection rate reached 87% among HCC patients in this study. Additionally, in our cohort, 93% of cases were classified as BCLC-C stage, 83% had macrovascular invasion, and 54% had tumor diameters exceeding 10 cm. Higher tumor burden and advanced disease stage may also enhance responsiveness to PD-1 inhibitors combined with antiangiogenic targeted therapy.21

Among patients with unresectable HCC, those demonstrating a favorable response or deeper tumor reduction to immunotherapy or targeted therapy are associated with improved clinical outcomes.22,23 Of note, a subgroup analysis from the phase 3 HIMALAYA trial elucidated that patients with deeper tumor reduction (25–100%) achieved a 5-year OS rate of 50.7%, highlighting the prognostic value of treatment response magnitude in this population.23 The radiographic response in our study also served as both a statistically significant prognostic marker (P < 0.001) and a successful conversion marker (P < 0.001). Strikingly, the surgical group in this trial achieved a 5-year OS rate of 73.9% (95% CI, 62.7–87.1). These collective results underscore that sequential curative-intent resection following the achievement of sufficient depth of therapeutic response may further improve long-term survival outcomes. We therefore propose that surgical intervention may be warranted for initially unresectable HCC upon reaching a depth of tumor reduction, as it confers the following benefits: (1) complete tumor eradication via R0 resection eliminates residual disease burden, establishing a foundation for potential cure; (2) surgical intervention reduces systemic therapy duration, thereby mitigating risks of acquired resistance and cumulative drug toxicities; and (3) postoperative pathological evaluation verifies preoperative drug sensitivity and provides an objective basis for formulating postoperative adjuvant treatment plans. Nevertheless, the assessment of response depth and the completeness of R0 resection may impact the outcomes of conversion surgery.

Current evidence regarding standardized criteria for pathological response evaluation and prognostic prediction following conversion therapy in patients with unresectable/advanced HCC remains limited.24 In a real-world cohort of the IMbrave150 trial, 38 tumors were resected from 32 patients (23 with PR and 9 with SD per RECIST v1.1) receiving atezolizumab-bevacizumab combination therapy.25 pCR occurred more frequently in PR-associated tumors than in SD-associated tumors (57.7% vs 16.7%; P = 0.034).25 Our study also clarified that among patients in the surgical group (n = 60) who achieved CR or PR based on radiological assessment, a higher proportion exhibited pCR on histopathological evaluation. Another study indicated that HCC patients who achieved MPR (defined as at least 70% tumor regression) following neoadjuvant immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy showed significantly superior recurrence-free survival compared to those who did not achieve MPR.13 Our study demonstrated that stratified pathologic response thresholds (0%, ≤50%, >50% residual viable tumor) were significantly associated with RFS (P < 0.001) and OS (P < 0.001), establishing the depth of pathologic response as a critical prognostic determinant in conversion therapy paradigms.

One study has indicated that hepatic decompensation is a critical predictor of poor prognosis in HCC patients receiving atezolizumab plus bevacizumab therapy, while effective antiviral treatment may prevent its occurrence.26 In this study, all patients with HBV or HCV infection received standardized antiviral therapy during conversion treatment, which effectively prevented hepatic decompensation. Only 4 cases of hepatic decompensation occurred in the entire cohort: 2 patients with gastrointestinal bleeding and 2 with massive ascites. The effective assessment of hepatic function, treatment of viral liver diseases, and timely management of hepatic decompensation have collectively enhanced the safety of sequential therapy, potentially contributing to improved therapeutic outcomes.

This study has several limitations that warrant further investigation. First, the single-center, single-arm cohort design without a parallel control group may introduce potential bias in efficacy evaluation. Second, the relatively limited sample size might compromise the statistical power of the findings. Third, the current study lacks fundamental research to explain the heterogeneous responses to conversion therapy among different patients. Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that we have preliminarily elucidated this issue at the single-cell resolution level in a separate study.27 Fourth, the lack of standardized subsequent treatment protocols for disease progression in both surgical and nonsurgical groups may introduce certain bias in OS analysis. Finally, a subset of patients may not achieve traditional pathological R0 resection because 28% of surgical patients experienced tumor recurrence within one year. Although the surgical indications (the criteria for successful conversion) in this study were determined through a multidisciplinary discussion, the standards we proposed in the article may not fully meet the requirements for accurately determining the appropriate surgical timing. More advanced clinical research is still needed to answer this issue.

The current trial elucidated that the sintilimab-lenvatinib combination represents a viable conversion therapy strategy for initially unresectable HCC with promising anticancer activity and tolerable safety. Notably, patients undergoing successful conversion followed by curative-intent resection achieved significantly improved long-term overall survival.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This prospective, single-arm, expansion phase II trial (Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ID: ChiCTR1900023914) enrolled consecutive patients with unresectable HCC at the Chinese PLA General Hospital between July 2019 and May 2023. The protocol-defined investigational framework comprised two sequential phases: Stage I evaluated protocol-defined conversion success rates and safety profiles encompassing conversion therapy, radical resection, and adjuvant regimens; Stage II implemented an expansion cohort with 5-year OS surveillance as the secondary endpoint. Patient eligibility criteria were comparable to those detailed in our previously published study.12

The trial adhered to International Council for Harmonization Good Clinical Practice guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki, with protocol approval by the Medical Ethics Committee of Chinese PLA General Hospital (Approval No. S2018-111-07). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to protocol-mandated interventions.

sec.title: Conversion therapy and decision-making on surgery
sec.p: All eligible participants received oral lenvatinib once daily (12 mg for body weight ≥60 kg; 8 mg for <60 kg) in combination with intravenous sintilimab 200 mg administered on day 1 of each 21-day treatment cycle. Tumor resectability was assessed by investigators at 6- to 8-week intervals, with the first evaluation conducted prior to the fourth treatment cycle. The definition of successful conversion must meet the following requirements: (1) Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) score ≤1; (2) Child‒Pugh liver function classification A or B; (3) no extrahepatic lesions assessed by PET-CT (or lung CT, bone scan, etc.) or extrahepatic lesions can be R0 resected, or extrahepatic lesions tend to be judged inactive by MDT; (4) intact vascular structure (both inflow and outflow) of the reserved liver; and (5) functional residual liver volume (FRLV) ≥ 45% for patients with chronic liver disease and ≥35% for patients without chronic liver disease.

Definition of R0 resection following sequential surgical resection after successful conversion therapy should meet the following requirements: (1) Intraoperative complete resection of all lesions (including tumor thrombi and active extrahepatic lesions) without grossly identifiable residual tumor; (2) Histologically confirmed absence of tumor cells at the resection margins of the excised liver tissue and vessels; (3) No residual tumor lesions detected on imaging studies (ultrasound, CT, or MRI; at least two modalities required) within 1–2 months post-operatively; (4) For patients with elevated preoperative serum tumor markers (e.g., AFP and DCP), normalization of these marker levels within 2–3 months post-operatively.28

Treatment-related adverse events were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.029, while surgical complications were classified per the Clavien‒Dindo grading system.30

sec.title: Postoperative histopathological assessment and adjuvant therapeutic stratification
sec.p: Under a standardized sampling protocol with rigorous pathologic evaluation, tumors ≤3 cm in maximum diameter were sectioned at 0.1 cm intervals, with complete circumferential sampling and histologic assessment of all cross-sectional surfaces. For larger tumors (>3 cm), comprehensive analysis was performed using a validated seven-point sampling protocol. Pathologic response depth was quantified by calculating the percentage of viable tumor within the entire resected specimen: pathologic complete response (pCR) was defined as complete eradication of viable tumor cells in the primary tumor bed, tumor thrombi, and lymph nodes; pathologic partial response (pPR) was defined as ≤50% residual viable tumor in the primary lesion; and pathologic nonresponse (pNR) was defined as >50% residual viable tumor or de novo lesion development.

Postoperative adjuvant therapy regimens were stratified by pathologic response: patients achieving pCR received sintilimab monotherapy for 6 months, those with pPR underwent sintilimab-lenvatinib combination therapy for 6–12 months, and pNR was maintained on dual-agent therapy for at least 12 months or adjusted secondary regimens by MDT.

Treatment strategies for recurrence or progression in surgical and nonsurgical groups: For surgical group patients experiencing recurrence during adjuvant therapy, as well as for nonsurgical group patients, the treatment should be adjusted to second-line regimens combined with appropriate local therapy. For surgical group patients with recurrence after discontinuation of adjuvant therapy, the original adjuvant treatment regimen should be reinstated.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the conversion success rate from initially unresectable HCC to resectable HCC. Secondary endpoints included OS, recurrence-free survival (RFS), the objective response rate (ORR) assessed by independent imaging review (IIR) per mRECIST31 and RECIST 1.132 criteria, R0 resection rate, pathological response, and safety profile.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All primary and secondary endpoint analyses adhered to the evaluable population principle, encompassing all participants who received ≥1 therapeutic dose. However, R0 resection rates and RFS analyses were restricted to patients undergoing curative-intent resection following successful conversion therapy. OS was defined as the interval from treatment initiation to death from any cause. RFS was measured from the date of surgery to first recurrence or death. Categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Survival outcomes were modeled through univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analyses. Survival trajectories were generated using Kaplan‒Meier methodology. To address immortal time bias, patients who underwent sequential surgery within 5 months of conversion therapy were defined as the surgical group, while those with conversion therapy exceeding 5 months or without surgery were classified as the nonsurgical group. Only patients with a minimum survival of 5 months were retained. We subtracted 5 months from the OS of all patients and subsequently performed Kaplan‒Meier analysis based on the redefined groups and adjusted survival time. This study employed inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) to adjust survival analysis outcomes, balancing variables including tumor diameter, portal vein tumor thrombus, degree of AFP decline during conversion therapy, treatment response, and maximum tumor shrinkage (mRECIST). Assessment of OS was performed using the IPTW-adjusted Kaplan‒Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models. Statistical significance was defined as a two-sided P < 0.05. All statistical computations were performed in R statistical software (version 4.3.0).
